articles.title: Chinese AI firms want Silicon Valley’s top minds. Poaching them won’t be easy
articles.content:
Chinese AI companies are hiring Silicon Valley-based engineers to work on their models, potentially tapping into the talent at American labs like OpenAI and Anthropic.

MiniMax, the Hong Kong-listed Chinese AI startup, currently has around 16 San Francisco-based job openings listed on its website, including for a research lead focused on developing its core AI model. The company is also recruiting specialists in finance, law, life sciences, and cybersecurity, as well as a lead recruiter to attract top AI talent in Silicon Valley and Seattle.

Moonshot AI, the Chinese company behind the Kimi AI model, is looking for U.S.-based  “solutions architects,” who will “help enterprise customers integrate its AI models into their businesses.”

American AI companies, with their deep pockets, have attracted global talent, including many Chinese engineers, by offering high compensation and opportunities to work on the world’s best models. In comparison, Chinese companies have so far largely relied on homegrown talent. Hiring in the U.S. reflects a strategic shift by Chinese companies as they look to compete and stay close to one of their most lucrative markets, experts said.

“Wanting to establish research teams in Silicon Valley makes perfect sense for Chinese AI companies seeking access to talent and the latest developments in the industry,” Cheryl Wu, a researcher in the economics of AI at Yale University and global think tank GovAI, told Rest of World.

Good Work and $$$

More than half of the world’s top AI researchers complete their undergraduate studies in China, a September study by research center Carnegie China said, based on the educational backgrounds of people who published papers at NeurIPS, one of the world’s leading AI conferences.

Yet the U.S. remains a global magnet for AI talent, the study concluded.

In 2025, the U.S. saw a net gain of 2,145 researchers while China recorded a net loss of 1,729, according to the analysis. 

China’s AI companies have been trying to lure top Chinese researchers at American AI labs to return home. One high-profile example is Tencent, which recruited former OpenAI researcher Yao Shunyu to lead its AI research.

Chinese companies are seeking “little geniuses” who have worked at companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, a headhunter recruiting for Chinese labs in the Bay Area told Rest of World, requesting anonymity as she is not authorized to speak to the media.

These attempts, however, have not had much success because Chinese companies often struggle to match the salaries paid by their Silicon Valley peers.

“It’s money. Chinese companies simply don’t have enough of it to offer competitive wages for talent,” said Wu, who published a report examining Chinese AI companies’ financing with research institute Epoch AI. “They have only recently begun raising more substantial funding and still lag far behind their U.S. competitors.”

There is a stark gap between what Chinese and American AI companies pay employees.

MiniMax spent $84.3 million on employee remuneration in 2025, equivalent to roughly $203,000 per person, based on its year-end head count of 415, according to its financial filings. The annualized remuneration costs of Z.AI, another Hong Kong-listed Chinese AI lab, in the first half of 2026 amounted to $140,000 per employee. Neither company disclosed a breakdown of pay for engineers or researchers, and both figures include share-based compensation and staff across all departments.

In comparison, OpenAI advertises annual base salaries of $250,000 to $445,000 for research engineers in San Francisco, before equity awards. Three Chinese researchers working in Silicon Valley say it’s common for their peers to get an annual compensation package worth more than $1 million.

As of September, China’s six leading AI firms collectively generated only about 10% of the combined AI-related revenue of OpenAI and Anthropic, according to Wu’s research.

“Career prospects are another factor. Even senior Meta engineers might accept a lower-ranking position to join Anthropic because of its work on frontier AI,” Wu said. “That makes it even harder to persuade top talent to join a lab whose models are just not at the cutting edge.”

Chinese tech companies are now ramping up their salary game. If an AI researcher had offers from OpenAI or Anthropic, ByteDance’s frontier model division Seed would try to lure them with a competing offer that’s 1.5 times higher, according to a person familiar with the team.

Wu Yonghui, a veteran AI researcher who worked at Google for 17 years, joined Seed as the head of research in early 2025. Seed currently lists 71 positions in San Jose, San Diego, and Seattle. 

But even with matching pay, three Chinese researchers working in the U.S. told Rest of World they preferred American companies for better work-life balance and the chance to work on frontier models. 

“I think most of the top Chinese talent would feel pretty comfortable in Silicon Valley; it’s the only other place where “996” isn’t really frowned upon,” Damien Ma, director of Carnegie China, told Rest of World, referring to the demanding work culture common in China’s tech industry, where employees work from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days a week.

Extension of the U.S.-China AI war

Washington has spent years restricting Chinese companies’ access to advanced Nvidia chips, and is scrutinizing their use of overseas data centers and cloud services. But no comparable restrictions prevent Chinese AI companies from establishing U.S. operations and hiring engineers there. 

Both Washington and Beijing are increasingly seeking to protect their most advanced AI technologies from each other.

The Chinese government proposed export controls on some of the country’s most advanced AI models, particularly those trained using the country’s “important data,” despite specifications.

U.S. officials and American AI companies, meanwhile, have accused Chinese AI labs of using unauthorized distillation techniques to replicate their models’ capabilities. On other sensitive tech fronts, like the semiconductor industry, the U.S. has already restricted some American engineers from working in Chinese facilities without a license.

While neither country has imposed a blanket ban on AI companies hiring researchers across borders, the growing competition over advanced technology could make talent recruitment another flashpoint.

“Given it is already so competitive, it doesn’t take much to imagine U.S. companies at some point capitalizing on U.S.-China competition and making national security arguments that will make it more difficult for Chinese labs to operate or to attract the best talent. Conversely, it’d be a similar dynamic if U.S. labs were operating in China,” Ma said. “This elite talent is by definition scarce; we are talking [about] like the top 5%–10% of people. Who wouldn’t want to hoard the best and the brightest for themselves?”

Chinese tech companies have previously faced U.S. restrictions that disrupted their American research operations. In 2019, telecom giant Huawei cut more than 600 jobs at its U.S. research arm, Futurewei, after Washington placed the company on a trade blacklist.

Not all Chinese AI companies want to hire in the U.S. China’s AI poster child, DeepSeek, continues to advertise research and engineering positions in China. It recently announced about 150 positions for engineers who would expand AI agentic and back-end infrastructure. In a 2024 interview, DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng said he hired mostly Chinese-educated people and believed the company itself could cultivate elite AI researchers.

Yale researcher Wu is skeptical that Chinese startups could attract enough top researchers to compete with America’s leading AI labs. “They may have plans to hire, but that doesn’t necessarily mean they’ll be able to find the people,” she said.

articles.title: N.Y. Lawyer Disciplined for "Antisemitic and Threatening Language" + "Physical Aggression" Towards "Jewish Artists for Palestine" Demonstrators
articles.content:
From a N.Y. appellate decision Thursday in Att'y Grievance Comm. v. Fernich (Judges Sallie Manzanet-Daniels, Tanya R. Kennedy, Barbara R. Kapnick, Kelly O'Neill Levy, and Matthew Parker-Raso); the respondent, Marc Fernich, is a prominent New York criminal defense lawyer, who represented, among others, Jeffrey Epstein, John Gotti, and Joaquin Guzman (drug cartel leader El Chapo):

The motion arises from an altercation between respondent and participants in a demonstration outside of the federal courthouse for the Southern District of New York on September 29, 2025. On May 27, 2026, the AGC served respondent with a notice and petition of charges alleging one charge of professional misconduct under Rules of Professional Misconduct (22 NYCRR 1200.0) rule 8.4(h), which prohibits conduct that adversely reflects on the lawyer's fitness as a lawyer. The parties have submitted a stipulation of facts, respondent's affidavit, and materials addressing aggravation and mitigation. Respondent admits to the stipulated misconduct, acknowledges the consequences of consenting to discipline, and agrees to a public censure.

On September 29, 2025, respondent, then 61 years old, was leaving a meeting at the New York County District Attorney's Office and was walking toward the Brooklyn Bridge. On Centre Street, he came upon a group of demonstrators in support of Palestine outside of the federal courthouse. Some demonstrators were singing and chanting, one played a guitar, and others held a banner reading "Jewish Artists for Palestine."

Respondent attempted to make his way through a circle of demonstrators, and admits that physical contact occurred as he attempted to proceed. Respondent grabbed a demonstrator's arm, pushed and grabbed others while moving through the circle, and engaged in heated verbal confrontation. The cellphone recordings of the incident also show respondent holding a demonstrator from behind with his arms around the person's waist, with the demonstrator shouting at him to remove his arms, respondent pushing and grabbing others, and respondent holding another demonstrator from behind with his arms around the individual's neck.

Among other things, respondent's threatening and antisemitic remarks included "Back off me, Kapo, Kike, Jew Boy!," "You fucking animal, you're worse than a fucking Muslim!," "You should have been aborted," and "You should have been thrown into an oven, I'd throw you in if I could!" He also said that the demonstrators' grandparents should have died in the Holocaust, as well as other inflammatory remarks invoking violence. Respondent remained at the demonstration for approximately one hour, until it ended.

At his deposition, respondent maintained that the video depiction of the incident was a compilation of cellphone recordings made by several individuals and that they were out of sequence and out of context. He asserted that the confrontation had not been one-sided; demonstrators had been linking arms, blocking his way, pushing back, and squeezing his genitals.

He also maintained that the recordings had purposefully omitted much of the physical contact and extreme anti-Israel and anti-Zionist rhetoric directed at him. Nonetheless, he recognized that the demonstrators had been exercising their constitutional rights to assemble and engage in free speech, and that his words and actions could not be justified. He was deeply ashamed of his conduct and expressed remorse.

The parties have stipulated that respondent's misconduct is aggravated by his substantial experience in the practice of law. They have also stipulated to considerable mitigation. Respondent has no prior disciplinary history. The incident was unrelated to his representation of a client or the practice of law, and did not disrupt a court proceeding. Respondent self-reported his misconduct to the AGC through counsel, cooperated with the AGC investigation, voluntarily appeared for examination, accepted responsibility, and expressed remorse and embarrassment for his actions. Fifteen character references described respondent as being well-regarded in the community and having character traits of honesty, integrity, and trustworthiness.

The record further reflects that respondent was experiencing significant medical issues at the time of the incident. He was recovering from a recent back surgery and experiencing significant pain, and had undergone emergency surgery for retinal tears shortly beforehand. He was also undergoing psychiatric treatment and taking medication for depression, anxiety, and ADHD. A report submitted by respondent's treating psychiatrist explains how the pain, emotional distress, and psychiatric symptoms respondent was experiencing may have contributed to his impaired judgment and agitation and, while respondent had been under his care for 13 years, he would never have expected him to engage in the kind of "angry and out-of-control conduct that he engaged in outside the Courthouse." Respondent, who has family in Israel, also maintains that the October 7, 2023 attacks in Israel affected him deeply and that his memory of those attacks caused his anger to boil over.

Under 22 NYCRR 1240.8(a)(5), the Court may resolve a disciplinary matter by consent where the submissions establish an admitted violation and an appropriate agreed-upon sanction. In support of the proposal for a public censure, the parties cite decisions imposing a censure for similarly offensive, abusive, and discriminatory remarks and other isolated misconduct (see e.g. Matter of Melogy, 233 AD3d 135 [1st Dept 2024]; Matter of Mukambetova, 204 AD3d 158 [1st Dept 2022]; Matter of Schlossberg, 192 AD3d 8 [1st Dept 2020]).

Respondent's use of antisemitic and threatening language, together with his physical aggression towards demonstrators, warrants public discipline. At the same time, the absence of a disciplinary history, the isolated nature of the incident, the medical and psychological circumstances, his cooperation, and his acceptance of responsibility supports the sanction jointly proposed. Public censure appropriately expresses the profession's condemnation of the relevant conduct while also recognizing the substantial mitigation.

Accordingly, the parties' joint motion for discipline by consent pursuant to 22 NYCRR 1240.8(a)(5) should be granted, … and respondent publicly censured….

Jorge Dopico and Raymond Vallejo represent the Committee.

articles.title: Despite being £61.7 million in debt, bankrupt MindsEye devs Build a Rocket Boy are splurging on legal action against "a coordinated campaign of negative online reviews"
articles.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
articles.content:
Administrators say "a substantial litigation fund is anticipated to arise"

Freshly published bankruptcy documents for perennially troubled MindsEye developer Build A Rocket Boy have spelled out the scale of the company's debt, with around £61.7 million owed to creditors. The documents also touch on founder Leslie Benzies and CEO Mark Gerhard's claims that MindsEye is the victim of an organised sabotage campaign. The company's leaders have apparently taken out even more loans in order to fund legal action against the suspected perpetrators, with the promise of a healthy payout. I'm not holding my breath.

BARB went into administration in September, with Opus Restructuring appointed to oversee attempts to salvage the insolvent business and ensure that creditors get their money back. Listed by Companies House on 16th November, and unlocked for reading today – just in time for the first crop of GTA 6 reviews on console - the docs consist of a notice of adminstrator's proposal and a statement of affairs. The latter features a breakdown of Build a Rocket Boy's assets and liabilities.

BARB's largest debt by far is the roughly £36.5 million owed to NetEase, publishers of Marvel Rivals. Asset manager Diameter Capital Partners are the second largest external creditor, having loaned BARB around £4.25 million. A further $19 million is owed to "group undertakings" – "group undertakings" meaning debts to parent companies, subsidiaries or fellow subsidiaries. Studio founder Benzies, meanwhile, is owed £1,158,167.05. Given that Benzies has been repeatedly accused of torpedoing MindsEye's fortunes by way of disruptive micro-management, I'm not sure many BARB staff would agree that he really deserves his million quid back at this stage, but that's what it says on paper. Smaller IOUs include £10,434.11 for Amazon Web Services, £634.36 for Unity, and a mighty £19.90 for OpenAI.

Build a Rocket Boy have been on a journey, it's fair to say. Announced in 2023, their flagship project MindsEye is a filmic GTA-ish action shooter initially billed as a full-fat demo for Everywhere, a game creation platform comparable to Roblox. MindsEye struggled to compel us before launch and did not find its people on release, with poor sales leading to layoffs even as BARB leadership insisted they could revive the game's fortunes.

The same leadership were subsequently accused by their own staff of "disastrously" mishandling the redundancies and enforcing "unbearable" crunch. Unionised BARB employees have now taken management to court for installing alleged surveillance software on their work PCs. The game's publishers Io Interactive noped out of the picture in March this year. Meanwhile, Benzies and Gerhard have thrown around accusations of a sinister espionage and sabotage campaign, carried out by unspecified perpetrators. They made a sort of revenge fantasy DLC pack about it, which our own Mark Warren characterised as we-already-have-Hitman-at-home.

The bankruptcy documents shed more light on these twists and turns. According to the administrators, BARB were "funded mainly by equity investment from institutional, strategic and venture capital investors over several funding rounds, including a $110m Series D round in 2023." This followed a £32 million investment in 2020, as reported by GI. The company grew significantly during MindsEye's creation to around 500 UK and overseas employees. According to a group income statement, the company posted sequential operating losses of £47.5 million for the period ending September 30th, 2025, and £63.1 million for the year ending December 2024.

The administrator proposals document also devotes some time to the aforesaid allegations of sabotage. "The directors formed the view that the game's commercial prospects may have been adversely affected by a coordinated campaign of negative online reviews and commentary," it reads. "The directors subsequently received information which they considered suggested the involvement of a number of third parties in organising and funding such activity and commenced litigation against some of those parties. The directors have indicated that such claims may be substantial in value, although the extent of any recovery remains uncertain and will be dependent upon the outcome of ongoing investigations, legal proceedings and asset recovery actions."

A later section vaguely alludes to the sum BARB leadership hope to recover. "Prior to the Joint Administrators' appointment, the Company had undertaken detailed investigations and had commenced litigation against several third parties, with the assistance of the Company's former legal advisers, Brandsmiths, in connection with matters described earlier in the Proposals," the doc reads. "The Joint Administrators consider the litigation potentially to be the largest asset of the Administration."

The document goes on that BARB management have "sought financial support from third party investors to fund the anticipated legal costs and expenses associated with the litigation", with some of these funding agreements already executed. "Further executed agreements and associated funding contributions are expected to be received, shortly, and a substantial litigation fund is anticipated to arise," it continues. The Joint Administrators are "currently engaging in the on-going litigation, progressing the funding arrangements entered into by the Company, and have assessed the merits of pursuing the litigation". They will liaise with relevant parties to "determine the most appropriate strategy for preserving and, where appropriate, realising value from this potential asset for the benefit of creditors and other stakeholders."

The doc doesn't name who, exactly, is being taken to court. As far as I'm aware, it isn't us. Anyway, it's good to know that the company who owe over £60 million are taking on more debt in order to pursue a histrionic grievance for which they have yet to supply any real evidence whatsoever.

articles.title: Columbia is keeping its gates closed, raising the question of what universities owe their neighborhoods
articles.author: @ljstprof
articles.content:
The Gaza war protests that overtook some colleges and universities in 2023 and 2024 have long dispersed – but one very clear remnant of the demonstrations remains at Columbia University’s Morningside Heights campus in New York City: a closed campus.

Columbia’s administration first shut the gates in April 2024, following pro-Palestinian rights protests and waves of police arrests. New York City politicians said that these disruptions were fueled by “outside agitators.”

Now, only students, faculty, staff and alumni with a school ID are able to enter Columbia’s quad.

Some of Columbia’s neighbors sued the university in January 2025, saying that the closure created a “six-block barrier between Broadway and Amsterdam Avenue from West 120th to West 114th Street” and violated the Americans with Disabilities Act and Rehabilitation Act.

A New York Supreme Court judge in Manhattan dismissed their suit on Nov. 10, 2026, saying that “even if Columbia previously granted unrestricted public access to College Walk, as it remained their private property, nothing prevented them from restricting access at any time.” The plaintiffs quickly appealed the decision.

Columbia has maintained that safety concerns meant it needed to close its gates, and that the campus is private property.

Nonetheless, in the past, Columbia allowed neighbors to cross the campus as a scenic shortcut through the neighborhood. Nearby nursery schools used the campus green as a place for children to explore and play.

As a college professor of law and political science, and an elected official in the western Massachusetts town where I teach, the Columbia campus controversy feels familiar. These “town-and-gown” disputes have, from time to time, raised questions about what universities owe the community beyond their gates.

Town-and-gown conflicts

From at least the 1950s until 2024, Columbia had an open campus policy. In 1953, New York City approved closing the campus’s central West 116th Street stretch to cars, with the understanding that pedestrians would be able to walk across the campus.

The recent closure stirred up tensions between the school and its neighbors. But such strains are as old as universities themselves. Some commentators suggest that conflict between universities and their surrounding communities can be traced back to medieval Europe.

“The early universities in cities such as Bologna and Paris took a very different form to the institutions we know today. They were loose communities of masters and scholars who lived amongst the people of the town,” the education historian Harley Richardson wrote in 2020.

Townspeople often resented those scholars and students because “They couldn’t understand the scholarly Latin spoken by the students” or whether “the long gowns they wore” were “intended to convey a superior social status,” Richardson wrote.

One of the most notorious town-gown incidents that turned violent occurred in Oxford, England, in February 1354 on so-called St. Scholastica Day, honoring an Italian saint who founded the order of the Benedictine nuns.

Trouble began in a local tavern when some students complained loudly and aggressively about the poor quality of the wine they were served. Things escalated when the tavern-keeper, who was also the mayor of Oxford, responded with insults. A fight broke out and drew in a large number of townspeople and students who rushed to the scene. It took the intervention of the king to restore order.

Conflicts between universities and their local towns or cities have also been very much a part of the story of higher education in the United States.

Most often these disputes have focused on issues like where a university should build a dormitory or whether it should pay fees to the city where it is located.

And as in England, these conflicts have occasionally turned violent.

One such incident happened in New Haven, Connecticut, in 1806, when riots broke out between Yale University students and locals who were on their way to church.

Universities’ civic responsibilities

What, if anything, do universities owe their communities?

The popular phrase “the ivory tower” captures one vision of a university. It suggests that universities serve society by being left alone to conduct research and educate students, disengaged from the larger community’s immediate concerns. In this view, people outside of universities benefit indirectly from the inventions and innovations that universities produce, as well as from the jobs they create.

Another vision, which came to prominence in the 1960s, called on universities to be good citizens of their surrounding communities. This view urged university leaders to invest in their neighborhoods.

Colby College, in Waterville, Maine, exemplifies this approach. It has spent US$265 million on construction and other investment projects over the past several years, with an eye on revitalizing its struggling downtown district.

Others schools, including the University of Notre Dame, the University of Pennsylvania, the University of Southern California and the University of California, San Francisco, have invested substantial amounts of money in developing their towns and cities and supporting neighbors. Trinity College in Hartford, Connecticut, for example, announced in September 2026 that it would pay for the full tuition, housing and meals for local residents who are admitted as students.

Some universities have been sending students out into the communities around them as one way to support their city. For example, Columbia Journalism School students are often tasked with developing a reporting project in a particular New York City neighborhood.

And some leaders in higher education now talk openly about orienting their schools toward the promotion of the greater good.

Closing gates or building bridges

A university investing in its surrounding community does not guarantee the end of tensions, which to me seem an inevitable part of the higher education landscape.

But when universities show their communities that civic responsibility is core to their mission, they build goodwill and offer a way of bridging divides when conflicts occur.

I don’t know how the Columbia campus dispute will resolve. But as newly elected New York State Assemblyman Eli Northrop observed: “Columbia is successful when Morningside Heights is successful and when the relationship between the neighborhood and the university is good.”
